_note: BIOLOGY ONLY. Compiled from general spearfishing-guide sources (not a validated regional survey), for the temperate US/Canada East Coast (roughly Cape Cod to the Carolinas). Depth, temperature, substrate and season of presence and how each species responds to water clarity. None of it is law - rules vary sharply by state (for example Massachusetts bans spearfishing striped bass outright, while New York and Rhode Island allow it), and none of that is encoded anywhere in this app.

species.note: The Northeast's headline gamefish - migratory, moves through rocky current-swept structure (walls, points) in spring and fall runs, thinner in mid-summer and absent in winter as it moves offshore/south. Banned for spearfishing in some states (Massachusetts) even where legal in neighbouring ones.

Blackfish - slow-growing, doesn't move far from home structure, sits tight in mussel-covered rock and is one of the easier East Coast species to approach. Moves to deeper water in the coldest part of winter.
Resident on reef, wreck and jetty structure through the warmer months, moving to deeper offshore water in winter.
Porgy - schools around reef and mixed bottom, common bycatch alongside tautog and black sea bass, easy to approach.
Fluke - a flatfish that wants open sand near structure rather than the structure itself, the same ecological role as California halibut on the other coast.
More a Mid-Atlantic and Southern species than New England - piers, jetties and reef structure, distinctive human-like teeth for cracking shellfish.

_legal_note: Legal rules live in legal/<JURISDICTION>.json and are merged in at run time. No legal pack exists yet for the US East Coast states, so this app will correctly show 'not researched' rather than any size or season claim - and the rules genuinely differ state to state (Massachusetts bans spearfishing striped bass and lobster outright; other states allow striped bass but regulate size and season).
